patterns: A provocative question or paradox in the first 2‑3 seconds that promises a single, timeless lesson from a classic work.
A quick list tease (e.g., “3”, “5”, “10”) that signals bite‑size wisdom, keeping the video under 30 seconds.
Contrast: ancient philosophy vs. modern problem, using a striking quote to bridge the gap.
Visually‑driven hook – a close‑up of an old manuscript or illustration that immediately draws curiosity.
Emotional payoff: end with a concise, actionable “try this today” statement that feels personal and empowering.
title_formulas: "[Number] SURPRISING LESSONS FROM [PUBLIC‑DOMAIN CLASSIC] YOU’LL USE TODAY"
"[ONE‑WORD EMOTION]: THE [PUBLIC‑DOMAIN BOOK] QUOTE THAT WILL CHANGE YOUR [NOUN]"
opening_3s: A rapid flip of a parchment page with a voice‑over: “What if a 19th‑century novel could solve your biggest stress?”
Show a stark black‑and‑white silhouette of a philosopher with text appearing: “Ever wondered why this ancient line still hurts?”
Begin with a bold on‑screen question: “Are you living the life you’re reading about?” followed by a flash of the original title page.
comment_themes: Viewers ask for deeper context about the author’s life and why the quote matters.
Requests for more concrete, daily‑action tips linked to the classic lesson.
Appreciation of the visual style that makes old texts feel fresh.
Desire for longer “list” videos that compile multiple short lessons.
avoid: Any medical, financial or dietary claims that sound like a miracle cure.
Quoting modern, copyrighted works or using other creators’ compilations.
Overly sensational language that promises unrealistic results (e.g., “lose 10 kg in a week”).
try_next: A 20‑second montage of Marcus Aurelius’ “Meditations” verses over city‑rush footage, ending with a one‑sentence daily stoic practice.
A “One‑Page‑ADay” series using public‑domain novels like ‘Pride and Prejudice’, each short revealing a single actionable habit.
A split‑screen debate where Socrates and Confucius (text excerpts) argue a current social issue, with captions guiding the viewer’s own stance.
